title: A little piece of the whole
question: How can one thing be shared fairly?
idea: A fraction names equal parts of one whole. Two equal parts are halves. Four equal parts are fourths.

math.title: One whole. Fair shares.
math.parentNote: 3 min: fold scrap paper. 9 min: draw and explain. 3 min: compare. Ask how Leo knows the parts are equal; let him point, fold, or speak.
math.intro: Imagine this rectangle is one whole picnic sandwich. To share it fairly, each person needs the same amount.
tasks: Two friends share one sandwich. Draw a line to make 2 equal parts. Shade one half.
Four friends share another sandwich of the same size. Draw lines to make 4 equal parts. Shade one fourth.
Which is more food: one half or one fourth of the same sandwich? Circle it. Tell someone how you know.
math.extension: Try it: fold a paper in half, then in half again. Open it. How many equal parts do you see?

reading.title: The picnic puzzle
reading.parentNote: 3 min: preview whole, equal, half. 7 min: read together, then reread. 5 min: discuss. Read aloud as needed; answers may be spoken.
paragraphs: Leo and Jo sit on a quilt. They have one big sandwich.
“Let’s share,” says Jo. Leo plans a cut. One piece would be big. One would be small.
“We would each have a piece,” says Leo. “But would we have the same amount?”
Jo points to the middle. “Let’s make two equal parts.” They cut there.
Now each friend has one half. The two halves make one whole sandwich. A fair share feels just right.

words.meaning: one of two equal parts of a whole

questions: Why would Leo’s first plan not be fair? Underline the words that helped you.
What did Jo change? Tell how the story shows two halves make one whole.

writing.title: Teach a friend to share
writing.parentNote: 3 min: tell an idea aloud. 4 min: draw and label. 6 min: write 1-3 sentences. 2 min: read back. Accept invented spelling or take dictation.
writing.intro: A friend has one whole sandwich for two people. Explain how to make a fair share.
writing.draw: Draw the whole sandwich. Show the cut. Label each half.
writing.check: Read it aloud. Did I explain equal parts? Did I start with a capital and finish with a mark?

answers.label: Math · 1
answers.text: A line through the center makes two equal regions. Either a vertical or horizontal cut works. Shade one region: one half (1/2). Diagonal halves are also valid.

answers.label: Math · 2
answers.text: A centered cross or three equally spaced parallel lines makes four equal regions. Shade one region: one fourth (1/4). Accept any four equal-area parts.

answers.label: Math · 3
answers.text: One half is larger than one fourth of the SAME whole. Two fourths cover one half. Folding twice makes four equal parts; the whole stays the same size.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: The planned pieces were different sizes. Evidence: “One piece would be big. One would be small.” Having two pieces alone does not make them halves.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: Jo chose the middle to make equal parts. The final paragraph says the two halves make one whole sandwich. Leo may also point to a drawing or fit paper halves together.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Example: “I would cut the sandwich in the middle. Each person gets one half. It is fair because the parts are equal.” Look for the idea of equal amounts; do not require this exact wording.

parentGuidance: Use two equal-sized paper rectangles as the wholes. A half of a small whole is not always bigger than a fourth of a large whole. Keep the wholes the same size today. The suggested 15 minutes includes talk and hands-on work, not a speed target. Take breaks between subjects.
